facts.text: The mantis shrimp can punch with an acceleration of over 10,000 times the force of gravity, creating cavitation bubbles that collapse with a flash of light reaching temperatures around 4,700°C—nearly as hot as the surface of the sun. This underwater shockwave is powerful enough to kill prey even if the strike misses.

facts.text: The Turritopsis dohrnii jellyfish can reverse its aging process by converting its adult cells back into their earlier polyp stage through cellular transdifferentiation, effectively restarting its life cycle when injured or stressed. This biological process allows individual specimens to potentially bypass death from old age, though they can still die from disease or predation.
facts.verification_note: Turritopsis dohrnii can indeed reverse its life cycle through cellular transdifferentiation from its medusa stage back to its polyp stage when stressed or injured, though this biological immortality doesn't protect it from predation or disease.

facts.text: When a pregnant mouse experiences stress, her female offspring will produce eggs that already carry molecular markers of that stress, affecting grandchildren that haven't even been conceived yet—a scientifically documented case of trauma being encoded across three generations simultaneously.
facts.verification_note: Studies have documented that stress exposure in pregnant mice (F0 generation) can affect the developing fetus (F1) and the primordial germ cells within F1 females that will become eggs for the F2 generation, resulting in epigenetic changes observable across three generations from a single exposure event.

facts.verification_note: Honey's low moisture content (around 17-18%), acidic pH (3.2-4.5), and production of hydrogen peroxide create an inhospitable environment for microorganisms, and archaeologists have indeed discovered preserved honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that remained unspoiled after thousands of years.

facts.text: The platypus is one of the few venomous mammals, with males producing venom through spurs on their hind legs that causes excruciating pain in humans and can kill animals as large as dogs. The venom contains at least 19 different peptides, some of which are unique to the platypus and produce pain that cannot be relieved by morphine.
facts.verification_note: All major claims are scientifically accurate - male platypuses do have venomous hind leg spurs, the venom contains multiple unique peptides and causes severe morphine-resistant pain in humans, and can be lethal to dog-sized animals.

facts.text: The bombardier beetle defends itself by mixing two chemicals in a special chamber inside its abdomen, creating a boiling spray that reaches 100°C (212°F) which it can accurately aim at attackers. The beetle avoids harming itself through a hardened, heat-resistant chamber lining and by releasing the explosive mixture in rapid pulses rather than continuously.
facts.verification_note: Scientific studies have confirmed that bombardier beetles produce a defensive spray reaching approximately 100°C through the mixing of hydroquinones and hydrogen peroxide with catalytic enzymes in a hardened reaction chamber, releasing it in pulses (up to 500 per second) to prevent self-injury.
